maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I may start my remarks by paying a particular tribute to the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) who, I think, is held in esteem by all hon. members in this house.
We heard him answer, with great tact and felicity, all questions hon. members wanted to ask him. We heard him discuss the problem of trusteeship for the seamen's unions, and, during the intercession, saw him try hard to find a private solution for that extremely serious problem which might have led to a settlement. We have seen him rise in this house to explain his position at the time of the seamen's strike or during the dockers' walk-out. He took a very firm attitude, and I think that all hon. members here are proud that Canada should have such a Minister of Labour.
I would be remiss, at a moment where an amendment is being discussed in connection with his department, not to take a few minutes in order to stress those facts.
It has been said, this afternoon, that the government had not taken all necessary measures to relieve unemployment. That statement is partly true and partly false. It seems to me, that to be fair and truthful it would be well briefly to list the various measures announced by the government since it came into power. All that legislation was more
Unemployment Measures Lacking particularly aimed at relieving winter unemployment and all unemployment in the near future, and some provisions aimed at putting an end to unemployment over a longer period.
All members will readily agree that unemployment is actually the most serious problem at the present time. It is the source of many of our difficulties as I will show later on.
Allow me to read a list that I put together very hastily showing what the government has done or intends to do in the near future in order to alleviate unemployment. It was never claimed in the house that these measures would altogether solve the unemployment problem.
Some special measures were first announced to help areas called designated areas. Those measures affected 35 areas-10 or 12 were added subsequently-where the federal government will pay 60 per cent of labour costs for winter works and provide an additional sum of $7 million for emergency winter works.
An assistance program has also been announced for new industries in those areas whereby income tax will only be collected three years after the new firms have been established, and special depreciation has been provided for new equipment and buildings.
I think those measures are already producing results in those areas. In my riding of Iles-de-la-Madeleine, for instance, if I may be allowed to refer to it for a moment or two, winter works for more than $600,000, will be carried out which will do away with all unemployment there for seven or eight weeks. Should weather permit, we might be able to extend the projects into January and February.
The government, after much difficulty, had its municipal aid legislation adopted. That measure will help municipalities to carry out immediately certain projects which otherwise would have been delayed.
The special allowance of $500 for those who build houses in wintertime will allow us, I think, to reduce unemployment during winter.
The important wheat sales now taking place will undoubtedly increase employment in the field of transportation and in certain allied industrial areas.
The new government policy concerning the importation and exportation of automobile parts will help the economy of this country.
The new regulation governing technical training will also help.
The new policy pertaining to assistance for older workers will stimulate the re-employment of workers 45 years and over and will likely allow a certain number of those workers to go back to work.

Unemployment Measures Lacking
The Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, by a more generous policy concerning loans, will help the economic development of some areas.
The announcement of an investment of $100 million in the Atlantic development board will help the Atlantic area.
The creation of a Department of Industry and of an economic board will probably, in the long run, enable the Canadian government to solve this problem.
I am not entirely satisfied with the situation and I do not think any of us is. But there are probably a number of proposals which will be brought forward and which will enable us to see the day when there will be in Canada what is called in other countries and has been called here full employment.
We have been talking about full employment for a long time in our country. I have before me a report published in 1945 under the title "Employment and Income". This report has been called the "white paper on full employment". Here is what we can read in it:

In setting as Its aim a high and stable level of employment and income the government is not selecting a lower target than full employment.

As far back as 1945, this was the policy of the government. Since then, there has been much talk about full employment and unemployment. And if the hon. members would look at the House of Commons debates index, they would notice that this has been the most discussed subject for five or six years.
In fact, a special committee on manpower and employment has been established in the Senate and sittings took place in 1960 and
1961.	This committee submitted a voluminous report on the employment problem.
The fact remains, Mr. Speaker, that even though one knows the unemployment problem, its details, its various forms, as an hon. member of the opposition mentioned this afternoon, a basic decision has never been taken, namely whether governments, federal and provincial, should interfere in the direction of the economy.
All kinds of solutions have been suggested, all aspects of the problem have been considered, but when one reads all these reports, one is always under the impression that there was a gap at a certain time and that the government was never able to make up its mind and really step into the economic field. I think that is the crux of the problem.
We could discuss ad infinitum the causes of unemployment and the solutions we think possible, but as long as governments, all of them, will not make up their minds to step
[Mr. Sauve.l
in in order to stem unemployment and apply a policy of full employment, Canada will experience, as she has in the past, long periods of unemployment.
All the reports I studied, especially the Senate report I just mentioned, reflect worry about what the economic situation will be between 1965 and 1975, when there will be a significant influx of people on the labour market.
That is the heart of the problem and it is up to us to decide whether we really want to step in. As long as we go on thinking that private enterprise can solve the unemployment problem all by itself, that important public works, unemployment insurance and assistance will be able to help the jobless for some time, we will never solve definitely the full employment problem.
Everybody admits that a certain level of unemployment is acceptable-although people who suffer from it do not-say 2 or 3 per cent, but a higher rate of unemployment, like ours, is not normal. Now I think that the unemployment situation in Canada is the source of other difficulties which are also very serious.
Unemployment in Canada is mostly rampant in the maritimes, in British Columbia and in Quebec. These are the three areas of this country which are usually hit the hardest by unemployment.
But I will point out, if I may, that it is these areas or these provinces which seem to have always some criticism to make with respect to the action or the inertia of the federal government. It is these provinces which find it difficult to get along with the federal government, and I believe that, as far as my own province, the province of Quebec, is concerned, unemployment and the economic situation of its population are probably the main cause responsible for the uneasiness which prevails in the federal-provincial relations and in the relations between French speaking and English speaking Canadians.
In my opinion, nobody questions the responsibility of the federal government to ensure full employment. It seems that it has been said a long time ago that full employment is at first a responsibility of the federal government.
On the other hand, some provincial governments are willing nevertheless to help relieve unemployment in their section and I believe it is urgent that both the federal and provincial governments agree on the policies which should be implemented in order to solve the unemployment problem.
The problem does not have the same acuteness throughout. Thus it is obvious that in Ontario, unemployment is less critical

than in the province of Quebec, the maritimes or British Columbia, and too many steps are taken by the federal government at the national economic scale, that is they apply indiscriminately to all the areas of the country, thus often creating a surplus of jobs in some areas while others suffer from under-employment.
I am glad that the government has decided to set up so-called "designated areas". It is a sign that the government now recognizes that certain districts are worse off than others in Canada and that certain nation-wide programs will not be as successful there as elsewhere. It still remains that those measures will not be effective unless there is close cooperation between the federal government and the provinces.
I should like to point out that we are no longer in the same situation as we were between 1945 and 1957.
At that time, the central government was powerful and the provinces did not question its jurisdiction in several fields. The provinces have come a long way since then.
Several provincial governments are well aware of local and regional problems. The federal government will then have to take the necessary steps to come to an agreement with the provinces.
In 1963, it is no longer possible for us, in Ottawa, to act as though we were always right.
Mr. Speaker, I could also take the economic council as an example. My remarks will probably be interpreted as a criticism of government policy, but I should like to say a word about that just the same.
I could say a lot of things about the role that can be played by the economic council which was set up recently. In particular, I feel that one of the two major aspects of economic activity has been neglected.
The economic council for the most part takes into account private enterprise which has an important part to play in economic activities, but public enterprise is practically always ignored.
Now, it is the federal, provincial and municipal governments, as well as crown corporations, both on the federal and provincial levels, which are responsible for the economic development of the country. And if private and public enterprises do not meet at the superior economic level to make decisions about economic planning, then public enterprise is being ignored, because the necessary intervention of the public powers in economic matters is being overlooked. This is exactly what I was saying earlier. This course was not chosen. On the contrary, it is still believed that only private enterprise can solve
Unemployment Measures Lacking our problems. Now, it has been proved that private enterprise is unable to do so and that far too much is expected from it. But private enterprise, assisted by public enterprise and co-operating with it, can succeed in reaching this level of economic activity which will ensure full employment.
That is what happened in Europe. The old continent went through the same phases as we did. Before the war, Europeans believed that private enterprise could solve any problem; yet, after the war, even private enterprise realized that it needed government assistance. In my opinion, the European experience is extremely valuable. Why, then, did we not take the same option here, in Canada? Because we refused to make a definite choice in favour of government intervention in the economic life.
I now have to blame the members of the opposition-I think I am entitled to it, since I have tried to be impartial. I would like when economic legislation is discussed, legislation meant to cope with unemployment or to promote the economic activities of the country that, the two main parties, among others, would agree on the urgency of improving the economic conditions in Canada, especially in the province of Quebec. As I said earlier, as long as in the province of Quebec unemployment will be twice as high as in Ontario or as long as the personal income per capita will be 37 per cent lower than in Ontario-and I do not want to continue along on that line-as long as we remain on a lower economic level, we will feel unhappy.
I was greatly pleased with the speech which the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) delivered last Tuesday. I would hope that his party would support him when he states that we, of the province of Quebec, consider ourselves as equal partners. Those are not the exact words he used but we would hope that everybody would have the same attitude towards us. At a time when we are discussing economic matters, I feel that his party should support the government so that we would not have to delay until the next session the adoption of legislation which is essential to the economic development of Canada and of the province of Quebec in particular since, as I said before, that is a basic condition of agreement between French and English Canada.
I did not like at all that part of the speech made by the hon. member for Three Rivers, who came back with the old line on mutual understanding. We heard all that from 1945 to 1960. The period of "bon ententisme", as defined by the hon. member for Three Rivers, is over and, to be perfectly honest, I am surprised that the English speaking press could find his speech praiseworthy.

Unemployment Measures Lacking
I think there they tried to shut their eyes. I could very easily tell you and we could very easily tell you that everything is getting along fine and that there is no problem, but I would be dishonest if I were to tell you that. I believe we should all work together, and that is important, because all members of this house are aware that there exists serious unrest in Quebec. There are in that province people who think it is possible to solve in some other way the problems now facing us.
Incidentally, let me tell you that people often confuse nationalism and separatism. There is certainly a nationalist crisis at the present time in the province of Quebec. We are probably all nationalists, that is we want the situation to improve in Quebec to a point where we shall really become equal partners with the rest of Canada.
We may be nationalists, but we are not separatists, and those who identify separatism with nationalism are doing a disservice to the cause of Canadian unity.
There are in the province of Quebec a small number of separatists. We know them and they have been identified. Maclean's magazine and the C.B.C. have made a survey, the results of which were published last week.
The problem has been set I think but it seems to me extremely important that we establish a distinction between nationalism and separatism.
When it is claimed, in this house or elsewhere, that all nationalists are separatists, direct offence is given to the people of Quebec.
I perfectly realize that most of my colleagues are beginning to understand the problem but I would not want us to put the matter off. On November 25, there will be here in Ottawa, an extremely important federal-provincial conference for the future of confederation. I believe that it is up to the federal government-I have said so outside this house-to take action in order to save confederation.
We want to become equal partners here in this country, but really equal. We have faith in Canada, we fought for Canada on several occasions and has a witness, General Foulkes, not said before the defence committee that the French Canadians, during the last war, had probably been the best soldiers?
We are in our own country, here; we want to be at home in the province of Quebec and in the other provinces of Canada but we want to feel at home everywhere.
We want to do our share, we realize now that in the province of Quebec we have to make exceptional efforts and that may be the reason why, at times, we are asking for a lot.

We shall get along, I think, if both sides have but one aim: keep Canada together, because Canada without the province of Quebec would not survive. And the province of Quebec, without Canada, would not survive either.
There is but one solution to our problems, that is to live together. We shall continue to have misunderstandings, to experience difficulties, that is normal; but I think that if we can overcome the present difficulties, we shall celebrate together confederation and we shall continue, French and English Canadians, to work for a better Canada. In my opinion, there is but one way to achieve this and that is to deal immediately with the fundamental problem, unemployment. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the government has already made an effort and that if, with the help of the hon. members, we can have that measure adopted, then we shall have done a great deal for Canadian unity.

We have today the same situation which, far from improving, has become worse since the hon. members opposite-

-have come into power. The hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine dealt with the problem mainly with regard to the province of Quebec of which he spoke very feelingly, and I commend him for it.
If we look at the figures issued by the dominion bureau of statistics and compare statistics for August and September 1962, with the figures for the same months in 1963, we find that in August last year there were
96,000	unemployed in the province of Quebec, whereas there were 97,000 in September.
This year, that is in 1963, in the province of Quebec, under a Liberal regime, in Ottawa as well as in Quebec, we still unfortunately, find Quebec reaching the highest level of unemployment, namely 108,000 in August 1963 and still the same figure in September last, that is 5.5 per cent in August and 5.7 per cent in September.

The hon. member said that our party, that we, of the opposition, should support the government and not cause delays in the passing, to use his own words, "of legislation essential to the economic progress of our country" which are brought forward.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
I have been looking over the subamendment. I think it would be unfair to say the members of the present administration are not conscious of the problem of unemployment. As a matter of fact, when they were on this side of the house they spoke of nothing else. They could think of nothing else and could find no other subject on which to entertain the house than the subject of unemployment.
Today they do not care to speak about it. It is swept beneath the rug. Unhappily, though, the problem is still with us; it has not been solved by those masterminds opposite. If anything, it is likely to be more serious than ever during the coming winter months, precisely because of the failure of the government to take effective new measures to deal with the situation. When I say hon. gentlemen who now grace the treasury benches have a concern for unemployment, I should have said they had a concern about unemployment when they were over on this side of the house. One of those who expressed the most concern was the gracious Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that at that time the hon. member for Essex East was the main critic of the official opposition in matters of labour, employment and unemployment. As a matter of fact, he made several contributions on this particular subject which are recorded in Hansard. I cite a few extracts at random from the inspired words of the hon. member for Essex East, now Secretary of State for External Affairs. I might say that he was vastly concerned with the problem, so much so that on the 2nd of February, 1960, as recorded at page 645 of Hansard, he had the audacity, I think, to single out Canada as "the one country in the western world where, in spite of our resources and great industrial capacity and the capacity of our people, there has persisted continuously since the fall of 1957 the most serious unemployment problem of any country in the western world".
Sir, if the situation then was as described by that hon. member, then I say it is every bit as serious now because statistics prove there has been no improvement since. In the course of the same speech the hon. member

Unemployment Measures Lacking said that this situation was an indictment of our society. I should like the hon. member who is now a member of the government, to note these words because they are words he could very usefully repeat to his colleagues in the cabinet now. At that time he said:
I say to this government, the same vigour that it demonstrated in the course of the elections, when it talked of unemployment, it ought now to demonstrate when it comes to consider what should be done about it.
The chickens are indeed coming home to roost, Mr. Speaker. I could use word for word the same flamboyant epithets which the Secretary of State for External Affairs was so fond of using when he sat on this side of the house to castigate the lack of action on the part of the government then. Let him now instigate action on the part of the government of which he is a member, that very government which rode into office on the promise that they would rid the country of its principal problem, unemployment. What have they done? In terms of effects and results they have done just about nothing.
With regard to the winter works program, the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) this afternoon related how that program had been initiated by the previous administration, how it had been ridiculed by members of the opposition at that time, how a great number, perhaps a majority of municipalities throughout the country availed themselves of its provisions, and how it had created year after year since its implementation hundreds of thousands of new jobs for Canadians. This one measure initiated by the previous government to combat unemployment achieved striking and complete success and has borne rich fruit for the citizens of Canada.
Yet at that time the hon. member for Essex East could find no other words to describe that splendid and successful program than "that anaemic child of the government". It might have been anaemic in the mind of the hon. member, but certainly in comparison with some of the measures the present government said they would implement, and never have, it was indeed a vigorous child that produced hundreds of thousands of new jobs. Some hon. members on the other side scoff at that. They do not seem to believe. Let them cite one single measure introduced by them which has produced hundreds of thousands of new jobs for Canadians. They have not produced a single one as far as I know.
I could go on at some length recounting the utterances of members of the government at the time they were in opposition with regard to the measures they would propose when they came into power. Again, on the 2nd of February, 1960, the hon. member for Essex East made certain suggestions. For


instance, he said that responsibility for unemployment must be transferred from the Department of Labour to the government as a whole, particularly to the Department of Finance, including the Bank of Canada, under a vigorous ministerial chairmanship.
I can understand why the government has discarded this proposal when one considers the dismal failure of the budgetary proposals made by the Minister of Finance to resuscitate, as he said, the Canadian economy. That is one proposal which members then in the opposition insisted upon strongly in order to restore our economy; but today there is not the slightest inkling that the government is anywhere near adopting such a proposal.
The opposition of that day said: Let us adopt a national advisory board on economic development. They have established something like that, but it has not produced any jobs yet. I can quote as my authority none other than the speaker who preceded me, the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve).
Another proposal made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was to set up a special parliamentary committee to deal with the problem of unemployment, and assess the facts. When some of the members now in the opposition propose the setting up of a parliamentary committee to deal with unemployment the only thing we hear is, "No, that is no good, because as the opposition you will use it in a partisan way,"-as if the hon. member for Essex East on that day had any other idea than to use the committee precisely in a political way. The proof of that is that today the government refuses to set up such a committee.
The opposition of that day were very fertile and prolific in proposing solutions to the problem. They said: Let us call a federal-provincial conference on unemployment. I know a federal-provincial conference has been called, but it is not to deal with employment or unemployment. It is to deal with relations between the provinces and the federal government, which have reached a very low ebb indeed since the 22nd of April last.
Here is another proposal made at that time which I commend especially to members of the cabinet. It was proposed by no other authority than the hon. member for Essex East that a leading businessman be appointed to provide leadership in supplying jobs. I think that would be a very good proposal and I have the name of a leading businessman, a chartered accountant by profession, to suggest. He is the present Minister of Finance. In a private capacity I think he could perhaps do a lot better than he has done as Minister

of Finance. 1 am sure of one thing: He could not do any worse, and he has got a lot of help.
The opposition of that time spoke of that anaemic child, the winter works incentive program. They were not satisfied with the
150,000	to 200,000 jobs provided every winter by that program. They said: Let us make modifications to the winter works program. Where are these modifications? I know the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) is looking at me as if to say I do not know very much. I know that in his wisdom and following the dictates of his advisers he has proposed that with respect to the winter works program in certain designated areas-and the subject of designated areas is a very touchy one-the federal contribution be increased from 50 to 60 per cent. As far as I can see, that is the main modification that has been brought forward by the government, which was going to revamp completely that great, successful program initiated by the Conservative government when it was in power and which has contributed greatly to the maintenance of a decent amount of employment throughout the country in the winter months.
These are some of the main proposals. There is one more proposal which is dear to the heart of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He also proposed that the excise tax on automobiles be abolished. Our government did that. It did not require a Liberal government to be in power for that to be done.
These are some of the measures that were proposed by the former opposition members now occupying the treasury benches. As you can readily see from the summary of the measures that I have put before you, Mr. Speaker, none of them has been implemented in an effective way by the present government, which has been noted not for its drive or its constructive proposals but more for its confusion and its dilly-dallying.

The Minister of Justice, when he was on this side of the house, was also quite prolific and proposed means to deal with unemployment.
I remember a brilliant speech he made at the time he was but the member for Laurier, on March 2, 1960, and which is to be found beginning at page 1651 of Hansard.
The hon. member for Laurier had proposed some 25 measures to remedy the unemployment situation. Well, his government has been in office for six months-it is no longer a matter of 60 days but rather of several hundred days-and the proposals the hon. member was enumerating at that time to deal with unemployment have not been
Unemployment Measures Lacking adopted, except those the Conservative government, which was in office until April of this year, did adopt.
I am quite sure the minister has not forgotten that eloquent and vibrant speech, and I do not have to insist too much and set down the proposals he put forth. The fact remains that, the moment these hon. gentlemen are given full authority to act, they seem to forget all about those suggestions, recommendations, measures and means. They hang on to obsolete ideas or extend a recovery program launched by the previous administration.
And even the present ineffable Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) who was then member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont, ventured to make some remarks on the unemployment situation. As we may see on page 4167 of the official record for May 23, 1960, he was shocked to see such a great number of people at the unemployment insurance office in the city of Montreal.
He had good reason to be shocked, but he might use his camera today and take the same photos-or even let him forget his photographer's talent for a few weeks and try the same experiment the next few months. He will see then that the situation remains exactly the same, because the government of which he is part has been unable to elaborate a program to remedy the present situation.
As we may read on page 4169 of Hansard for May 23, 1960, the present minister said then:
What did the Conservative government do to try and maintain employment at a reasonable level in Canada?
And now we may ask: "What did the present government do to try and maintain employment and jobs in this country at a reasonable level"?
And the hon. member added:
What interest did this government show in avoiding a deterioration of the employment situation to the point I mentioned a few moments ago when quoting the last figures?
Indeed, what interest does the Liberal government show in this problem?
And the hon. member said further:
To what extent did the government listen to the admonitions and warnings which it so frequently heard from the opposition?
Mr. Speaker, why do those gentlemen, who have a good memory and are not without intelligence, not pull themselves together and recall the words and suggestions they made at the time when they were sitting on this side of the house?

speechtext:
When I have completed my remarks, Mr. Speaker.

I think, Mr. Speaker, I should continue along the line on which I started. There is another prominent member of the administration who had a lot to say about unemployment. He was, Mr. Speaker, the golden haired boy of Liberalism, the white hope; he has become a bit gray now, I will admit. I am referring, of course, to that brilliant economist the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). He had quite a few comments to make before he entered this house, and particularly before he became a member of the administration.
In October, 1960, Mr. Speaker, he published in the Toronto newspapers, as for instance the Toronto Star, what he called a "bold program" to solve the problem with which this country is now faced, mass unemployment. The minister then stated, as an example, that mere talk could only waste time and what was needed was action. Imagine those words coming from that source. He said that what was needed was a concerted policy to attack this evil thing that sapped the will and the spirit, not only of those who have no jobs, but all the rest of us who may become fearful for the future. At that time the minister urged a concerted policy; but what indication has he given to us today of a concerted policy, a comprehensive policy, something that makes economic sense? He has not given us any indication of that. He has given us exactly the contrary.
At this time I believe it would be helpful to table a copy of "Walter Gordon's Solution". This appeared in the Toronto daily Star for Saturday, October 15, 1960. "Twelve Golden Rules to Achieve Full Employment", by Walter Gordon, the then rising star of Liberalism and noted economist, who has now become the quiet and subdued Minister of Finance. I should like to table these rules, because I am sure that they would serve as a reminder to the government of its sins of omission and commission and its absolutely incomprehensible indifference to the admittedly grave problem of unemployment. They talked a lot about this problem in the days before the election, Mr. Speaker, but now that they are in a position to do something about it, what do we get? There has been no action, no sensible action. I wish to table these 12 golden rules which are Walter Gordon's solution to the problem. Well, we know what that problem is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The hon. member realizes, of course, that he cannot table that


kind of document. He can leave it on the table if he wishes, but it cannot form a part of Hansard.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: I am satisfied to leave it on the table. I hope that hon. members opposite will go around the table and take a look at it. Possibly it will be impressed upon their minds.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Read it.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
Yes, I will read it a little later.
I was going to say that in those days, contrary to his present practice, the minister was quite loquacious. He used to make a lot of speeches during the years 1960, 1961 and 1962 concerning what would be required to solve unemployment. For instance, at one time he said that one of the reasons for unemployment was tight money. Well, Mr. Speaker, I seem to recall 1955 and 1956. I seem to recall businessmen in this country complaining bitterly over the fact their sources of credit had been cut off by the banks and the financial institutions, as a result of the policies of the government. It was this same tight money government that was driven out of power, you will recall, in 1957. The Minister of Finance describes tight money as one of the causes of unemployment. Indeed, it was, but he failed to mention the origin of that tight money, Which was the policy of the former minister of finance, Mr. Walter Harris.
The minister went on to say that what was needed to bring about an end to unemployment was really not an end of tight money but it was, on the one hand, the cutting of taxes, and on the other hand the balancing of the budget. He said we had to decrease our deficit, and that if the budget had been balanced in 1958 or 1959, either by increasing taxes or by reducing expenditures, the need for such a rigidly tight money policy would have been greatly removed. Then he added that neither of these alternatives would have been popular, but they would have been wise.
Then, the Minister of Finance made a speech in Quebec city which was reported in the Toronto Star of November 24, 1960. He called for a cure for unemployment, and I quote from the newspaper article:
Temporary cuts in personal income taxes, lower interest rates and a reduction in the premiums on the Canadian dollar are the fastest and most effective cures for unemployment, economist Walter Gordon said last night.
The present government, despite the expert advice freely given by men like the Minister of Finance, when he was outside the house or sat in opposition, has not seen fit to cut the income tax or other taxes. As a matter of fact, we know only too well that, contrary to

the promises it made, there has been an increase in personal income tax. We have also seen the monstrous imposition of a tax on building materials and production machinery, and we have had the Minister of Finance forecast that his budget deficit will be the highest peacetime deficit in Canadian history.
There is the difference between the pragmatists, men like the Minister of Finance, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and a few others, and the theorists, the idealists, the impractical dreamers; and in this government it is the impractical dreamers who have got the upper hand, because how else could the government have got the country into the rudderless mess which the London Economist spoke about some few days ago?
These are some of the attitudes the government has chosen to adopt, and under those circumstances it is not surprising that there has been no improvement in the economic and unemploment situation. To illustrate that, I quote from the dominion bureau of statistics' bulletin of October 25, 1963 where it states:
Employment declined by an estimated 181,000 to
6.565.000	between August and September.
That is the net result, a decrease in employment under a government that was elected to promote and expand economic activity. It is a dismal record.
The Montreal Gazette of September 14, 1963, stated that the Liberals' job rise was off target and that unemployment continues to persist on the seasonally adjusted basis at between 5 per cent and 6 per cent of the labour force. There is no improvement there, and it is no surprise that the Prime Minister stated not very long ago that unemployment was such a fundamental problem that the federal government could not cope with it. It is only too apparent that the present government cannot cope with the problem.
The situation would be infinitely worse if some of the forward looking, progressive measures that were adopted by the previous government had not been implemented. I speak for instance of the winter works incentive program, which has been continued by this administration, and which has provided
150.000	to 200,000 jobs a year since 1960. I speak also of the launching of the vocational and training program on a scale such as this country had never seen before.
We also called a conference of leaders of industry and labour to meet with the government, and one recommendation made by that conference led to the establishment of the national productivity council. What has this government seen fit to do about that council? It has abolished it. That was an instrument which did good and important work to increase the productivity of our
Unemployment Measures Lacking workers, and that is one of the main requirements if we are to keep abreast of our competitors. I think the Minister of Trade and Commerce will agree with me there.
We also set up the Senate manpower inquiry, and through successive budgets adopted sensible, reasonable incentives for industry through tax concessions of various sorts that gave a good impetus to industry in so-called surplus labour areas. Those measures were infinitely more logical and better applied than the hit and miss incentives for designated areas announced recently by the Minister of Finance, and which have caused a great deal of confusion among organized and established industries. The case of Brantford is only one in point. Just a few days ago the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. Greene) pointed out how unjust it was for regions such as Pembroke to get the advantages, when a sister town in Renfrew South did not benefit from them. The same holds true for many other areas throughout the country.
It was our government which also launched the great export drive that pushed Canada's exports to new all time highs. This was due to new, liberal and sensible ways which we adopted to finance trade exports, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce knows that if our exports are showing increasing gains it is due to those types of measures.
One of the measures which was ridiculed by members of the government when they sat in opposition was devaluation of the dollar. Everybody knows that devaluation, adopted by the previous government, was an act of great courage unparalleled in political government in Canada-because it was adopted in the middle of an election campaign-has brought great benefit and was a major incentive to exports.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Adopted? It was forced on you.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext:
The Secretary of State seems to think that is not so, but let him read some of the words of his colleague, the Minister of Finance when he wrote his treatise, "Troubled Canada", in which he advocated devaluation as one of the measures that had to be taken.
The measures now being put forward by this government are weak and anaemic. They do not respond to the gravity of the situation. The Minister of Labour has announced his nine points program, but this afternoon the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) pointed out the weakness of that program. As another masterpiece of economic recovery we had the budget of June 13, the main features of which were increased taxes; and now there has

Unemployment Measures Lacking been evolved, by the brains trust that surrounds members of the government, the municipal loan development fund. This is a measure of doubtful economic impact because it imposes new charges on the municipalities that they can ill afford to bear.
The works to be financed by the municipalities under that fund are works which, by their very nature, will be tremendously costly, and most municipalities have already reached a borrowing point beyond which they can ill afford to go. The government hopes to have the municipalities and their taxpayers finance this plan to cure a problem which, if it is to be cured, must be approached on a comprehensive and co-ordinated basis by the government, and that is why most financial critics do not agree with it. Only today John Meyer had an article about it in the Montreal Gazette, and said he felt the municipal loan fund would not provide the jobs which the government expects it to, and would place new burdens on the municipalities.
Members of the government made a lot of hay, or shall we say, a lot of noise about the national economic council.

I regret, Mr. Speaker, that the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne), the father of the economic council, is not in the house tonight.
I have noticed the well-justified criticism of that measure by the hon. member from the Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve).
With much fanfare, the President of the Privy Council brilliantly introduced that legislation in the house and had it passed. That newly established council is one of the organizations of our country. However, the President of the Privy Council maintains a complete silence on the matter. Is he ashamed of it? Why does he not submit a report on the business of that council?
That council was designed with the idea of co-ordinating all activities and "live forces" of the country in order to achieve full employment. Mr. Speaker, we have not seen anything up to now which could justify such hope.
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion, if we want to solve the unemployment problem, we must not aggravate our relations with our neighbours to the south, which is what the gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches are doing now. On the contrary, we must strive to resume friendly relations with that great country so that agreements can be reached, and we have not been given any indication of that so far.
We must also set up a better system of consultations with the provinces about unemployment as well as economic matters. I

would suggest that a conference be called specifically to study and recommend measures to be taken with regard to unemployment and economic development.
To that end, we could propose appropriate amendments to the winter works program, creating thus, as I said a short while ago, many jobs throughout the country.
For instance, instead of having only the designated areas benefit from the federal contribution of 60 per cent towards the cost of labour, that measure should be extended to all sections of the country and thought should also be given to the possibility of having the federal government pay for part of the cost of machinery and materials used by the municipalities in their winter works program. That would surely be an efficient way to fight unemployment.

speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member but his time has expired.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, one of the great wonders of mankind is that one never becomes too old to learn. We note today that after six or nearly seven years on the treasury benches, during which period the present official opposition, and particularly their front benchers, took the attitude that there was no unemployment problem in this nation and repeatedly refused to recognize the existence of unemployment as a problem in our nation, they have suddenly discovered now that there is a problem of unemployment.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: That is a lot of tripe.

maintopic: LACK OF MEASURES TO DEAL WITH UNEMPLOYMENT
speechtext: There are many ideas on how government should be carried on, Mr. Speaker, and the idea of the previous government as regards the unemployment question was what is known as "government by heads in the sand". We now note, as I say, that hon. members opposite have withdrawn their heads from the sand, as the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) has just demonstrated, and discovered that there is such a thing as unemployment in Canada. Having spent such a long time without noticing this fact, it seems that the hon. member is only now catching up on his reading, because despite what he considers and describes as a very serious problem of unemployment, he used the better part of his 40 minutes to recite and review speeches and books written by Liberals during the past six years.

I am glad to see that he is at least catching up on his reading in that regard.

I was greatly surprised this afternoon when the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr) chose as his topic for this motion of non-confidence that of unemployment. I think it is somewhat ironic that the hon. member for Ontario, who was minister of labour during the years when unemployment was so great a problem, when it grew and grew in size to monumental proportions, should come here after six years of being unable to contain or solve the problem and now criticize the government of this day for not having completely solved the problem in the six months during which they have been in office, despite the fact that each one of those six months has shown a decrease in unemployment in this country.
Unlike those who subscribe to the "heads in the sand" theory of government, we in the Liberal party recognize that unemployment is still a problem in this nation, a problem which we inherited last spring. Indeed, it is a major and tragic problem. In my view there is nothing so important to the dignity of the working man in this country as the matter of finding a job. I can think of nothing more tragic than a man with a family to support who is willing to work, who wants to work, but who cannot find work. I suggest that this government has taken a great number of measures, some of which, as the hon. member pointed out, have not yet borne fruit, because these things cannot all be accomplished in six months. But they have taken very significant steps to curb unemployment and create new employment. Just to mention some of those steps in passing, there is the extension of the winter works program, which has been altered to make it much more effective. We have incentives to new industry, such as the tax holiday and increased depreciation; and I think another very significant step is the municipal loan fund, which can result in a great deal of extra employment in this coming winter. Perhaps the most significant thing of all which has been accomplished by the new administration in this regard is the very coming into power of this government, which has restored business confidence in the country.

There is no question but that the wheat sales have helped create some employment. There is also no question that the wheat sales have helped to create an atmosphere which will encourage business to expand and commence new enterprises, which will in turn create employment. The government of indecision which went out of office last spring was one which did not inspire this business confidence, and as a
Unemployment Measures Lacking consequence we were not able to have an atmosphere wherein new jobs became plentiful.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that if we were to dissect this question of unemployment and analyse it we would find, in looking at the problem as a whole right across the country, that the disturbing thing is that there are large and severe pockets of unemployment. This matter was mentioned by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher) earlier today. Unemployment is not spread evenly across the country; there are certain areas in which it is a very serious problem. By the same token there are many non-skilled workers amongst those who are unemployed. On the other hand, there are jobs in some areas going begging for lack of skilled workers. There is also the problem of the worker whose skill has become unusable because of technological change in industry, and who today is unable to find employment.
With reference to this question of unemployment in certain areas, I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the government's program in establishing the Department of Industry and area development incentive is of very significant importance. I would further suggest, speaking as a maritimer, if I may be allowed to do so, that the funding of the Atlantic development board and the revitalizing of that organization by enlarging its membership is a very progressive step toward helping create employment in the maritime provinces.
Turning to the question of skill of the workers of this country, the program of vocational training started by the previous government was a good one. I would hasten to point out that it was not a new or original concept, as vocational training had been participated in by federal governments as far back as 1919. Nevertheless I think we need to extend and develop the training and retraining of our workers. It is important to make full use of the national employment service. One of the more significant accomplishments of the present government, something which I hope will merely be an initial step in a new direction, is the assistance which has been granted to older workers in order to encourage employers to employ people over the age of 45. This is new territory for government in this country, and I think this initial step will certainly be helpful. I think the question should be closely studied because much more can be done to encourage the employment of those who as a class, have greater difficulty in obtaining employment. We should attempt increasingly to assure that young people do not enter the labour market until they have

Unemployment Measures Lacking the necessary skills. There is certainly a continuing problem, not only in this country but in every major country in the western world caused to a large extent by changing technological processes, and the fact that fewer workers are needed today to handle machines than in the past. I wish to point out that assistance on a strictly regional basis is no permanent answer because it does not really solve the problem; it merely transfers employment from one area to another. One example is the competition for shipping between the St. Lawrence seaway and the Atlantic ports. I do not see that merely transferring the handling of goods from the port of Halifax, which has handled them in the past, to some inland port will help the over-all economy in any way, particularly when we consider the fact that the goods will be carried from Toronto or some other port to the west by ships which are foreign-owned and that wages will go to foreign seamen rather than to employees of the C.N.R.
Sometimes, of course, the transfer of labour can help, for example when it creates an immediate area market which in turn can create new jobs. Nevertheless, wholesale retraining and the provision of an effective and realistic education program is the only long range answer to unemployment. This should be taken together with the point to which I referred earlier-keeping young people out of the labour market as far as possible until they have acquired skills. I will be the first to admit that this calls for much more investigation and participation by the government than has hitherto been the case because, of course, there are obvious pressures-a young person cannot readily stay at school if his family economic circumstances are such as to make it necessary for him to leave school in order to find whatever employment is available.
I think the answers lie, also, in the field of the export and manufacture of new types of goods. We must export more than we have in the past and, as has been pointed out many times in this house, this is tied up with the foreign ownership of such a large proportion of industry in this country. In addition, we must see to it that we manufacture, here in Canada, types of goods which we presently import from other areas. These measures must at all times be linked with the realization that employment should be shared among as many people as possible. Walter Reuther, who is perhaps the most able labour leader in the United States, has recognized that labour today, both in his union and elsewhere, must follow a policy of less overtime and a larger working force. Employment must be spread, and spending power must be spread.
[Mr. Regan.l

I think it is important that both unions and management in Canada should keep this concept in mind; unions in reaching their collective agreements must try not only to protect those who are already employed, but to recognize the position taken by Mr. Reuther and see to it that the way is open for as many people to be employed as possible.
I wonder if I might turn for a moment to the maritime area and the maritime economy. I agreed with many of the remarks made today by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). He mentioned that, in the past, military spending has been used to assist financially the economy of certain areas. I think that is true. I think it was done on a large scale under the previous Liberal administration. I will point to the building of Camp Gagetown in New Brunswick at a cost, I am told, of about $40 million. Ever since, that camp has pumped a great deal of energy into the economy of the province of New Brunswick. There is no doubt that the basing of a large portion of the Royal Canadian Navy in Halifax has helped develop the economy of that city. Over the years, this military spending has given Halifax the buoyancy to develop its economy still further. With each passing year the economy has become more diversified and in better over-all condition. The presence of the navy and the existence of other military bases in the area led in turn to the establishment of the Fairey Aviation Company, when the Liberal government was in power, and the Cossor plant, both large employees of labour, and to the modernization of the shipyards. These companies, together with the government, created in turn an immediate market in the Halifax area which enabled that city to reach a sufficient size to attract further industries. Although our economy would be in a sorry state if military expenditures were withdrawn at the present time, nevertheless the development of our economy is such that, with each passing year, it becomes more self-sufficient.
I must say I strongly disagree with the hon. member for Port Arthur in at least one respect. He made some comments about the shipyards at Halifax being inefficient. I believe he attributed those comments to someone else. I suggest the Halifax shipyards can hold their own with any in Canada. They are the shipyards which first built destroyers in this country. They have not only been the leaders in this industry, but in time of war they undertook all kinds of difficult repairs under the most adverse conditions that could be imagined.
Turning from the home area I should like to comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) suggesting that to a large extent the combating of

unemployment should be left to the provinces. At the risk of being branded a centralist, I cannot agree with this notion at all. We have a centralized economy. Workers are transferred by many companies from province to province and from one coast to the other. Goods manufactured in any part of Canada are marketed throughout the entire nation, and to combat unemployment in an economy of this type I suggest we need centralized direction of the measures being taken. I do not say the battle against unemployment should be fought only by the federal authorities. Certainly, the provincial governments have a large responsibility. But the measures taken must to a very large extent be given centralized direction from Ottawa. Unemployment insurance payments and family allowance payments have provided a cushion against recession in the past, along with other measures, and prevented the economy from sinking into depressions such as existed in the thirties. However, we must strive to find new ways of lessening the impact of major employment changes both in Canada as a whole and in specific areas. Whenever it is necessary because of large scale changes in employment and types of employment, it must be the role of government to see to it that we phase out old programs and phase in new ones so that the blow to the economy is not as serious as it might otherwise have been.
I submit that this government has brought forward good new measures and policies. It has begun the monumental task of overcoming unemployment in this country, a task which involves the dignity and security of every Canadian worker. Let us continue this battle until it is successful and place Canada in a position to profit from new sales and expanding trade in an era when living standards are rising throughout the world.

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to cut short a member who was so amusing. I am afraid I have left most of my best jokes at home. However, if my Liberal friends across the way follow their usual habit some of the things I may say favouring the former administration are liable to meet with as much merriment as the last speaker's explanations did.

Unemployment Measures Lacking
To begin with, I should like to point out to all hon. members that the Conservatives have been very restrained with regard to the question of Canada's unemployment problem. I am sure that most of us have a genuine concern for those people who are unable to find work for short or long periods of time, and I have no doubt that over the last several years most members of the house have had this feeling. There is a difference, however, between taking up the subject with the prime objective of trying to add something to government plans which may assist them, and taking up the subject because it happens to be a good political football, no matter what the consequences to the unemployed.
It does not take much memory for those of us who have been in the house in the last five or six years to recall the fact that unemployment was an almost daily subject of questions from the opposite side of the house. At that time the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin), now Secretary of State for External Affairs, had his own bureau of statistics which he quoted daily at great length, and every day in one form or another he brought up the question of unemployment. I need not remind the house that the Chair was not exactly strict. The government had an overwhelming majority and we had a Speaker who was very kind and tolerant. The objective was at all costs to avoid any pretence or show that the opposition was being strangled. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that nothing short of strangling would have stopped the hon. member for Essex East bringing up the subject of unemployment every day.
He did not bring it up in a manner calculated to put before the government of the day some helpful solution or hint as to policy, some course of conduct that might aid or ease the situation. Every day his questions were so framed as to try to give the people of the country the idea that there was unemployment in ever increasing numbers and that the government was doing absolutely nothing. In short, if ever there was a prolonged, sustained and deliberate attempt to undermine the confidence of the people in the government, the opposition of that day was responsible for such an attempt. I suggest it would do hon. members a lot of good to look at the present situation and the restrained way in which the opposition has considered this question, and contrast the way the former government used to handle the situation as compared with the attitude of the present government. Because, if they do, they will then have some idea of why the opposition has chosen to bring up the subject of unemployment on a supply motion, so that there can be a full and complete debate.

It can be said of a subject such as unemployment that it is so wide ranging there is some possibility that some of us may miss the target, and that there are so many aspects that some of them will not be discussed in detail. On the other hand, this debate does provide scope for those hon. members who wish to put forward ideas involving positive schemes to help the government in creating more, better paying and longer lasting jobs for Canadians.
If we are to consider whether there is merit in any scheme so brought forward, I think it is not out of place for me to bring to the attention of the house what I consider to be the general scheme and plan of attack that the previous administration had been following for several years. Certainly a little reminder along this line seems to me to be absolutely essential, bearing in mind the speech made by the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher). That hon. gentleman has quite a command of the English language. He has a habit of speaking like a college professor, almost humble at times but at the same time seeming to exhibit great authority with regard to the subject, as one who has done considerable research and who is thinking deeply about the problems besetting us.
I confess, Mr. Speaker, that in listening to his remarks today, part of them did seem somewhat like an analysis of some of the problems of unemployment in this country, but I suggest that it was all too shallow. The hon. member made a long speech which touched but gently and very lightly on some of the most obvious headings under which this subject can be discussed, without probing deeply to find out if any of these topics had a bearing on unemployment, which had the strongest bearing, which needed government attention and which had had the most government attention. Certainly the hon. member made a speech which sounded very wise, and I am sure it will be taken to heart for about as long as he spoke; because it sounded good. There was much more of art than matter in his speech.
The question of unemployment can be discussed under several headings. I can only speak of the actions which were being taken by the government at the time I entered the house in 1958. I can well recall when the unemployment situation started to get better. The short term project of pouring government money into housing was the first step taken. Here was a way that jobs could be provided immediately and results achieved at once for government funds spent. At the same time the government tried to press on with public works projects. Some which had been planned before were speeded up, and

every department scraped around to try to find more government projects which could be proceeded with immediately, instead of in the years to come.
I will admit that those are short term measures. There was some unemployment in 1958. In fact, it soon became apparent that as the effects of automation hit this country year after year, we were going to continue to have a serious unemployment problem for some time. Automation was throwing people out of work faster than we could put them to work. At the same time, the new and revised industries in other countries, such as Germany, Italy and Japan, were flooding world markets and pushing us out of our traditional selling places. They were going farther than that. They were making serious inroads into Canadian markets, so that our own manufacturers had a more difficult time trying to hold their own, without considering expansion.
This is the heart of the problem, automation, Mr. Speaker. In order to compete successfully against their competitors, Canadians had to put in that type of machinery and institute that type of process which their competitors had. This required smaller and smaller quantities of labour to produce larger and larger quantities of goods. At the same time, the market was shrinking and we had ever increasing demands for jobs. Certainly, no one in the government of that day took the problem lightly. I sometimes felt that some people did not grasp the full impact of the size of the problem. However, many minds worked very hard on it. I may say, sir, that there were some good debates on the subject and some worth while ideas were brought forth. I can honestly say that I believe every avenue of governmental activity, every method of government assistance to industry that sounded at all practical, was taken up. Some of these schemes were put into force, while others were merely in the planning stage.
While providing this new machinery to meet automation, we had to concentrate on the problems of Canadian businessmen in getting the necessary capital. This was at a time when our country had its balance of payments difficulties. There were new and increased demands, and yet heavier borrowings in world markets. We set up planning boards combining business, labour and government, to study how we could attack the problem. We increased the powers and the lending capacity of the industrial development bank to try to ease the money situation. We provided small loans for businessmen. We instituted a winter works program to try to spread the work around the year. We increased farm loans and brought in various 28902-5-280
Unemployment Measures Lacking extensions to farm legislation in the feeling that if the farm economy is healthy it helps the whole economy of the country. In fact, no avenue of short or long term assistance was overlooked.
The shipbuilding industry was hard hit, so we put in shipbuilding subsidies. The coal mines of Nova Scotia were in danger of closing so they were given rail subsidies. There was a feeling that, the greater the total development wealth of the country the better was our chance of surviving as an industrial nation. A program of national development was therefore instituted. There were roads to the north, new airports, new government buildings to open up new possibilities and fields of wealth. There were the forest access roads to open up new forests.
Co-operation with the provinces was not overlooked. Since this is a federal system and the provinces have their responsibilities, powers and opportunities to take care of so many of these problems, the provinces themselves were given a larger share of tax revenue to enable them to carry out broad, ambitious schemes. We had to attack unemployment, not remotely but in every manner in which it could be influenced by governmental activity, every potential activity in the country.
I should like to refer to the extension and expansion of the efforts of the Department of Trade and Commerce, which was one more cog in the strengthening of this machine. It is no accident that the Department of Trade and Commerce increased the number of its representatives abroad. It was the result of careful planning that brought these representatives home to train them in new roles and send them out to these new countries with a new dedication, a new purpose and a new spirit. No longer were they acquiescent representatives, but active, aggressive salesmen alert to the opportunities for Canadian businessmen.
Along with these opportunities for sales, the government assumed a greater responsibility. It was not a case of saying: Here is your chance for a sale, make it if you can. Certainly some of these potential sales carried a great deal of risk. There was a chance the customer would not be able to pay. You can always find more customers if you can give credit. The government was responsive by helping to give export credits insurance to those who made their own scheme. All of these measures were directed toward the industrial development and expansion necessary to provide jobs.
There were other methods taken. There are other problems to be faced. We had a lot of depressed areas. Special legislation was introduced to try to spread the benefits of

Unemployment Measures Lacking government assistance across the nation in an equitable way. We found that in coping with the demands of automation for new machinery, we had to provide new pools of labour. Canada had been a supplier of raw materials for years, and suddenly we found ourselves in a machine age. We had to buy the new machines and provide the money to do it. Then we found we had to supply the skilled workers, and we did not have them. It came as a bit of a shock to find that Canadians were amongst the poorest educated people in the world. It had always been so easy to make a good living in this country, in this land of opportunity, that there was not the pressure on young people to develop skills. Once we found ourselves in this era we had a call for skilled help, just as they had in Europe. We found we were unable to
provide it. While every day there were long columns in the newspapers for jobs wanted, people searching for work, there were other long columns of employers desperately searching for skilled workers that we could not provide.
This, of course, gave rise to the training scheme. While education is a provincial responsibility, it became apparent that the federal government would have to intervene if we were going to meet this problem. We had to take on that responsibility as part of the job of getting Canada rolling and ready to take its place in this new industrial age.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put.
